title: Pipes and Filters
summary: Connect commands with pipes, cut out lines with head and tail, count with wc, and keep a copy of a stream with tee.
intro: A pipe, `|`, connects one command's stdout to the next command's stdin. Tools built for this are called filters: they read stdin, keep, change, or count what passes through, and write the result to stdout. Chaining a few small filters answers most questions about a file in one line.

steps.title: Connect commands
steps.body:
`a | b` runs both commands at once, and everything `a` prints flows into `b` instead of to the screen. `b` reads it as its stdin, so it needs no file name.

```bash
head -n 3 fruits.txt | tail -n 1
```

`head -n N` keeps the first N lines, and `tail -n N` keeps the last N. `tail -n +N` starts at line N and keeps the rest, so `tail -n +2` drops a header line. Together they cut out any range of lines.

When a pipeline would start with `cat file`, give the file to the next command instead: `head -n 3 file` beats `cat file | head -n 3`. It does the same job with one process fewer, and the command still knows which file it's reading. Save `cat` for when it really concatenates several files.

examples.title: Same result, fewer processes
examples.prompt: Print the first three lines of `employees.csv`, with and without `cat`.
examples.code:
head -n 3 employees.csv
echo "---"
cat employees.csv | head -n 3
examples.explanation: Both print the same three lines: the header and the first two rows. In the second, `cat` reads the file and `head` reads `cat`'s output through the pipe, so two processes do one job. Handing the file to `head` directly is shorter and does less work.

examples.title: Skip the header
examples.prompt: Print the first three data rows of `employees.csv`, without the header.
examples.explanation: `tail -n +2` prints from line 2 to the end, which is every row without the header. `head -n 3` keeps the first three of those. Read a pipeline left to right: each command works on what the one before it printed.

examples.title: Count anything
examples.prompt: Show the first names in the `src` folder, then count all of them.
examples.code:
ls src | head -n 3
ls src | wc -l
examples.explanation: When its output goes into a pipe, `ls` prints one name per line, so any line tool can work on a listing. `head -n 3` keeps the first three names, and `wc -l` counts every line it receives: `src` holds 6 entries, its two folders included.

practice.prompt:

1. Start at the right line with `tail -n +N`.
2. Pipe the result into `head` to keep three rows.

Check runs it on two different score files.

Expected output:


steps.title: Count with wc
steps.body:
`wc` counts lines, words, and bytes. With no option it prints all three, then the file's name. Options pick the counts you want: `-l` for lines, `-w` for words, and `-c` for bytes.

```bash
wc -c fruits.txt
```

Give `wc` a file name and it prints the name too. Feed it the file through `<` or a pipe, and it prints just the number, ready to use.

`wc -l` really counts newline characters. A last line without a newline at its end isn't counted. `echo -n` prints its text without the newline, which shows this, and is also how you print a label and a count on the same line.

```bash
echo -n "fruits: "
wc -l < fruits.txt
```

examples.title: All three counts
examples.prompt: Count the lines, words, and bytes of `poem.txt`, then just its lines and words.
examples.explanation: Plain `wc` prints lines, words, and bytes, in that order, then the name. `-l -w` keeps lines and words, still in that order whichever option comes first. The blank line between the stanzas counts as a line, so the poem has 9.

examples.title: Just the number
examples.prompt: Count the lines of `access.log` with and without its name, then count the names in this folder.
examples.code:
wc -l access.log
wc -l < access.log
ls | wc -l
examples.explanation: With the name as an argument, `wc` prints the name after the count. Through `<` it prints the number alone. `ls | wc -l` counts the names in the folder: this lesson's files, the `src` folder, and `main.sh`, your script, which sits beside them.

examples.title: Label and count on one line
examples.prompt: Print a label and a count on one line, then count text that has no newline.
examples.code:
echo -n "lines: "
wc -l < app.log
echo -n "no newline" | wc -l
echo "one newline" | wc -l
examples.explanation: `echo -n` prints `lines: ` without ending the line, so the count from `wc` lands right after it. `echo -n "no newline"` sends text with no newline at all, and `wc -l` counts 0. A plain `echo` ends its text with a newline, which counts as 1.

practice.title: Log stats
practice.prompt:
Print how many lines and words `app.log` has, each on its own labeled line.

1. Print `lines: ` and the line count of `app.log` on one line.
2. Print `words: ` and its word count on the next line.

Check runs it on three different logs.

Expected output:

```text
lines: 62
words: 445
```
practice.starter:
# TODO: print lines: and the line count of app.log on one line

# TODO: print words: and its word count on the next line
practice.solution:

wc -l < app.log
echo -n "words: "
wc -w < app.log
hints: `echo -n` prints a label without ending the line.
Feed the file with `<`, so `wc` prints only the number.
`wc -w < app.log` prints just the word count.

steps.title: Longer pipelines and tee
steps.body:
Build a long pipeline one stage at a time: run the first command, check its output, add the next stage, and run it again.

`tee FILE` copies its stdin to the file and to its stdout, like a T-joint in a pipe, so you can save what flows past and keep going. `tee -a FILE` appends instead of overwriting.

```bash
head -n 2 fruits.txt | tee picked.txt | wc -l
cat picked.txt
```

A pipe carries stdout only. Errors skip it and go straight to the screen. `|&` sends stderr down the pipe too, the same as `2>&1 |`.

A pipeline's exit status is its last command's. So a failure early in the pipeline goes unnoticed, which the strict mode lesson fixes later with `set -o pipefail`.

examples.title: Stage by stage
examples.prompt: Build a pipeline that prints lines 16 to 20 of `access.log`, counting after each stage.
examples.code:
head -n 20 access.log | wc -l
head -n 20 access.log | tail -n 5 | wc -l
head -n 20 access.log | tail -n 5
examples.output:

Once the counts look right, drop the `wc -l` and read the lines themselves. Checking each stage catches a mistake before the pipeline grows around it.

examples.title: Save mid-stream
examples.prompt: Save the last 50 lines of `access.log` while counting them, then append one more line with `tee -a`.
examples.code:
tail -n 50 access.log | tee recent.log | wc -l
head -n 1 recent.log
echo "end of sample" | tee -a recent.log
wc -l < recent.log
examples.output:
50
203.0.113.64 - - [03/Oct/2026:14:51:38 +0000] "POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1" 201 1775 "https://shop.example/account" "Mozilla/5.0 (iPhone; CPU iPhone OS 18_6 like Mac OS X) AppleWebKit/605.1.15 (KHTML, like Gecko) Version/18.6 Mobile/15E148 Safari/604.1" 0.265
end of sample
51
examples.explanation: `tee recent.log` writes the 50 lines into the file and passes them on, so `wc -l` still counts 50, and `head -n 1 recent.log` shows the file kept them. `tee -a` adds its line to the end of the file instead of replacing it, and prints that line too, so the file ends with 51 lines.

examples.title: Stderr and pipes
examples.prompt: Pipe a failing `ls` into `wc -l` with `|` and with `|&`, then run it alone.
examples.code:
ls nope.txt | wc -l
echo "pipeline status: $?"
ls nope.txt |& wc -l
ls nope.txt
examples.errorIncludes:
ls: cannot access 'nope.txt': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access 'nope.txt': No such file or directory
examples.explanation: The first `ls` writes its error to stderr, which skips the pipe and goes to the screen, so `wc` gets nothing and prints 0. The pipeline's status is `wc`'s, 0, even though `ls` failed. `|&` sends stderr into the pipe as well, so `wc` counts the error as 1 line and none of it reaches the screen. The last `ls` runs alone, so its status, 2, becomes the script's, and the exit badge shows it.

recap:
- `a | b` sends `a`'s stdout into `b`'s stdin. Filters read stdin and write stdout.
- `head -n N` keeps the first N lines, `tail -n N` the last N, and `tail -n +N` everything from line N on.
- `wc` counts lines, words, and bytes with `-l`, `-w`, and `-c`. Feed it through `<` or a pipe to get just the number.
- `echo -n` prints its text without a newline.
- `tee FILE` saves a copy of what flows past and passes it on, and `tee -a` appends.
- A pipe carries stdout only, and `|&` adds stderr. A pipeline's status is its last command's.
- Give a file straight to a command instead of starting with `cat file |`.
